subject: IRS
question: Examine the consequences of the first and second Hijrah to Abyesinia.
modelAnswer:
Note: "Abyesinia" is a misprint for Abyssinia (Ethiopia, al-Habashah).

Background: because of severe persecution of the Muslims by the Quraysh in Makkah, the Prophet (SAW) advised some of his companions to migrate to Abyssinia, whose Christian king, the Negus (an-Najashi, Ashamah), was known for justice.
• First Hijrah (about the 5th year of prophethood, 615 CE): about 11 men and 4 women, including 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter. They returned after hearing a false rumour that the Quraysh had accepted Islam.
• Second Hijrah: a larger group of about 83 men and 18–19 women, led by Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. The Quraysh sent 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah with gifts to demand their return. Ja'far explained Islam and recited part of Surah Maryam; the Negus wept and refused to hand them over.

Consequences:
1. Safety of the Muslims: the emigrants escaped persecution and were able to practise Islam freely.
2. Preservation of Islam: a group of believers was kept safe outside Makkah in case the community there was destroyed.
3. First spread of Islam outside Arabia, and the first official contact between Islam and Christianity, marked by mutual respect.
4. Diplomatic victory: Ja'far's defence before the Negus defeated the Quraysh delegation and humiliated them.
5. Sympathy of the Negus: he protected the Muslims, and according to Islamic tradition he later accepted Islam; the Prophet performed the funeral prayer in absentia for him.
6. Increased Quraysh hostility: angered by their failure, the Quraysh intensified persecution, leading to the boycott of Banu Hashim in Shi'b Abi Talib.
7. Preparation for the Hijrah to Madinah: it showed that migration for the sake of faith was possible and acceptable.
8. Marriage of the Prophet to Umm Habibah (daughter of Abu Sufyan), contracted while she was in Abyssinia.
9. The emigrants returned in groups, the last with Ja'far at the time of Khaybar (7 AH), strengthening the Muslim community in Madinah.

subject: IRS
question: Examine the activities of Khadijah bint Khuwailid (R.A) to the success of the Prophet (SAW)'s mission.
modelAnswer:
Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA) was a noble, wealthy and respected businesswoman of the Quraysh, known as at-Tahirah (the pure). She employed Muhammad to trade on her behalf in Syria, impressed by his honesty (al-Amin), and proposed marriage to him. They married when he was 25 and she about 40, according to the common report. Her contributions:
1. First person to believe: she was the first to accept Islam, giving the Prophet immediate support at home.
2. Comfort and reassurance after the first revelation: when he returned from Cave Hira trembling, she covered him and assured him: 'By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, help the weak, serve your guests and assist those in hardship.'
3. She took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a learned Christian, who confirmed that what came to him was the same angel (Namus) that came to Musa.
4. Financial support: she spent her wealth freely for the cause of Islam, supporting the Prophet so he could devote himself to the mission, and helping poor Muslims and freeing slaves.
5. Support during persecution: she stood by him through the hostility of the Quraysh, including the three-year boycott in Shi'b Abi Talib, where she shared the hardship despite her status.
6. Emotional and moral support: she was a loving, loyal and wise companion who gave him peace at home.
7. Family: she was the mother of most of his children: al-Qasim, 'Abdullah, Zainab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah.
8. Example to women: her faith, generosity and loyalty made her a model for Muslim women.
Her death in the 10th year of prophethood, in the same year as Abu Talib's, was so painful to the Prophet that the year was called 'Am al-Huzn (the Year of Sorrow). He continued to honour her memory, calling her one of the best women of all time.

subject: IRS
category: Life and Achievements of the Khulafa Rashidūn
question: Analyze the procedure of the election of Caliph during the Khulafa'u ar-Rashidun.
modelAnswer:
The Prophet (SAW) did not appoint a successor by explicit designation (according to the Sunni view), so each of the four rightly guided caliphs (al-Khulafa' ar-Rashidun) came to office by a different procedure. All were based on consultation (shura) and the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah).

1. Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (11–13 AH): after the Prophet's death, the Ansar gathered at the Saqifah (hall) of Banu Sa'idah to choose a leader. Abu Bakr, 'Umar and Abu 'Ubaidah went there. After debate (the Ansar proposed 'a leader from us and a leader from you'), 'Umar pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr, and others followed (the special bay'ah). The next day the general public gave their bay'ah in the mosque. This was election by consensus of the leading companions.

2. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (13–23 AH): Abu Bakr, during his final illness, consulted senior companions (such as 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf and 'Uthman) and then nominated 'Umar in a written testament. The people accepted and gave their bay'ah. This was nomination followed by public approval.

3. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (23–35 AH): when 'Umar was fatally stabbed, he appointed an electoral council (shura) of six companions: 'Ali, 'Uthman, 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, az-Zubair and Talhah. They were to choose one of themselves within three days. 'Abd ar-Rahman withdrew his candidacy, consulted the members and the people of Madinah, and chose 'Uthman, who then received the general bay'ah. This was election by an electoral college.

4. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (35–40 AH): after 'Uthman was assassinated, the people of Madinah, including many companions, urged 'Ali to accept the caliphate. He accepted reluctantly and received the bay'ah publicly in the mosque. Some (e.g. Mu'awiyah in Syria) refused to pledge until 'Uthman's killers were punished, which led to civil strife.

Principles shown: no hereditary succession; consultation (shura, Q 42:38); merit, piety and seniority in Islam; consent of the people through bay'ah; flexibility of method.

subject: IRS
question: Enumerate the major events of the Prophet (SAW) from birth to Prophet-hood.
modelAnswer:
1. Birth: Muhammad (SAW) was born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant ('Am al-Fil, about 570 CE), traditionally on Monday 12 Rabi' al-Awwal, into the clan of Banu Hashim of the Quraysh. His father 'Abdullah died before his birth; his mother was Aminah bint Wahb.
2. Nursing: he was given to Halimah as-Sa'diyyah of Banu Sa'd to be nursed in the desert, where tradition reports the opening (splitting) of his chest by angels.
3. Death of his mother: Aminah died at al-Abwa' when he was about six years old.
4. Care by his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib, who died when he was about eight.
5. Care by his uncle Abu Talib, who raised and protected him.
6. Journey to Syria at about 12 with Abu Talib, when the monk Bahira at Busra recognised signs of prophethood in him.
7. Shepherding: he tended sheep for the people of Makkah.
8. Harb al-Fijar (the Sacrilegious War): he took part as a youth, gathering arrows for his uncles.
9. Hilf al-Fudul (the League of the Virtuous): he joined this pact to defend the oppressed and uphold justice.
10. Reputation as al-Amin (the trustworthy) and as-Sadiq (the truthful).
11. Trade for Khadijah to Syria, and marriage to Khadijah at about 25.
12. Rebuilding of the Ka'bah (about age 35): he settled the dispute among the clans over who would replace the Black Stone, by placing it on a cloak which the leaders lifted together.
13. Seclusion and meditation (tahannuth) in the Cave of Hira on Mount Nur, especially in Ramadan, and true dreams.
14. Prophethood: at about 40 (610 CE), in Ramadan, Angel Jibril brought the first revelation, 'Iqra' (Read!) (Surah al-'Alaq 96:1–5).

subject: IRS
category: An Overview of the Umayyad and Abbasid Dynasties
question: Account for the differences of 'Kuttab' and 'Madaris' schools in the early history of Islam.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with Islamic education; 'An Overview of the Umayyad and Abbasid Dynasties' is used as the nearest, since madaris flourished in that period.

Kuttab (pl. katatib): the elementary Qur'anic school. Madrasah (pl. madaris): an institution of higher learning, which developed later (e.g. the Nizamiyyah of Baghdad, founded by Nizam al-Mulk in 1067).

Differences:
1. Level: kuttab was elementary (primary); madrasah was higher/advanced (secondary and tertiary).
2. Pupils: kuttab taught young children; madrasah taught older students and scholars.
3. Curriculum: kuttab taught reading, writing, memorising the Qur'an, basic Arabic, simple arithmetic and the basics of worship. Madrasah taught advanced subjects: fiqh (jurisprudence), hadith, tafsir, usul al-fiqh, kalam (theology), Arabic grammar and literature, and sometimes mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.
4. Venue: kuttab was held in the teacher's house, an open space or an annex of the mosque. Madrasah had its own purpose-built buildings with lecture halls, libraries and student hostels.
5. Teachers: a kuttab had a single teacher (mu'allim); a madrasah had many specialist scholars (shuyukh, professors) and administrators.
6. Funding: kuttab was funded by small fees and gifts from parents; madaris were funded by endowments (awqaf) and by rulers and wealthy patrons, and often gave stipends, free lodging and food to students.
7. Organisation: kuttab was informal; madaris were formal, with a structured curriculum, a hierarchy of staff and certificates (ijazah).
8. Time of origin: kuttab existed from the earliest period of Islam (even before Islam for writing); madaris became widespread from the 10th–11th centuries (Abbasid/Seljuq period).
9. Purpose: kuttab gave basic religious literacy; madaris trained jurists, judges (qadis), teachers and administrators.

subject: IRS
category: The Distinction between the Makki and Madani Suwar
question: Examine the features of Makkan revelations.
modelAnswer:
Makkan (Makki) revelations are the surahs/verses revealed before the Hijrah (about 13 years). Their features:
1. Emphasis on Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and condemnation of shirk (idolatry).
2. Belief in the Hereafter: resurrection, the Day of Judgement, Paradise and Hell are described vividly.
3. Prophethood and stories of earlier prophets and nations (e.g. Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Musa) as lessons and warnings.
4. Short surahs and verses, especially the early ones (e.g. most of Juz' 'Amma).
5. Rhythmic, poetic and powerful style, with rhyme (saj') and strong appeal to emotion and reflection.
6. Frequent oaths by Allah's creation (e.g. 'By the time' (al-'Asr), 'By the sun', 'By the fig and the olive').
7. Form of address: often 'O mankind' (ya ayyuha an-nas) rather than 'O you who believe'.
8. Huruf al-muqatta'at (disconnected letters, e.g. Alif Lam Mim) begin most such surahs (except al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, which are Madani).
9. Most verses of prostration (sajdah) are in Makkan surahs.
10. Story of Adam and Iblis appears (except in al-Baqarah).
11. Every surah containing the word 'kalla' (by no means) is Makkan.
12. Moral and ethical teaching: honesty, kindness to orphans and the poor, condemnation of infanticide and fraud.
13. Absence of detailed legislation: no detailed laws on inheritance, jihad, criminal punishments or state affairs (these are Madani).
14. Refutation of the polytheists' arguments and consolation of the Prophet and believers under persecution.

subject: IRS
question: Evaluate the implications of the major classification of knowledge in Islam.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with the classification of knowledge; 'The Islamic Concept of Ibadah' is used as the nearest, since seeking beneficial knowledge is an act of worship.

Major classifications:
1. By source: (a) revealed or transmitted knowledge ('ulum naqliyyah/shar'iyyah), from the Qur'an and Sunnah: tafsir, hadith, fiqh, tawhid, Arabic as a tool; (b) rational or acquired knowledge ('ulum 'aqliyyah), obtained through reason, observation and experiment: mathematics, medicine, astronomy, natural sciences, logic.
2. By obligation (al-Ghazali): (a) fard 'ayn, knowledge every Muslim must have (beliefs, how to pray, fast and live lawfully); (b) fard kifayah, communal obligation: if some members of the community acquire it, the rest are freed from the obligation (e.g. medicine, engineering, agriculture, advanced jurisprudence).
3. By value: praiseworthy (mahmud) knowledge that benefits people, and blameworthy (madhmum) knowledge that harms (e.g. sorcery).

Implications:
1. Unity of knowledge: since all knowledge comes ultimately from Allah, religious and secular sciences are not opposed; both are valued.
2. Seeking knowledge is a duty and an act of worship: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim' (hadith; Ibn Majah). The first revelation commands 'Read' (96:1).
3. Individual responsibility: each Muslim must learn basic religious knowledge (fard 'ayn).
4. Communal responsibility: the community sins if no one acquires essential professional and scientific knowledge, which encourages development (doctors, engineers, scientists).
5. Moral direction: knowledge must be used for good and lead to God-consciousness (taqwa). Harmful knowledge is discouraged.
6. Scientific progress: this outlook encouraged the golden age of Islamic science (e.g. al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, al-Biruni).
7. Educational planning: the classification guides curricula that combine religious and modern subjects.
8. Respect for scholars: 'Are those who know equal to those who do not know?' (Q 39:9).

subject: IRS
category: The Observance, Types, and Values of Salāt
question: Enumerate the features of Friday prayers.
modelAnswer:
Salat al-Jumu'ah (the Friday prayer) is commanded in Q 62:9: 'O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade.'
Features:
1. It is obligatory (fard 'ayn) on every adult, sane, free, male, resident Muslim who is able to attend. It is not obligatory on women, children, travellers, slaves or the sick, though they may attend; if they attend, it suffices in place of Zuhr.
2. It replaces the Zuhr prayer on Friday and is performed at Zuhr time (after the sun passes its zenith).
3. It consists of two rak'ahs, with the recitation read aloud.
4. It is preceded by two sermons (khutbahs) delivered by the imam standing, with a short sitting between them. The khutbah includes praise of Allah, salutations on the Prophet, Qur'anic verses, admonition and prayer for the believers.
5. It must be performed in congregation (jama'ah); it cannot be prayed alone. Schools differ on the minimum number: 40 (Shafi'i, Hanbali), 12 (Maliki), 3 besides the imam (Hanafi).
6. It is usually held in a central (Jami') mosque.
7. The adhan is called; since 'Uthman's time, many communities have two calls.
8. Recommended acts (sunnah): taking a bath (ghusl), wearing clean/best clothes and perfume, using siwak, going early, reciting Surah al-Kahf, abundant salawat on the Prophet, and reciting al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun (or al-A'la and al-Ghashiyah) in the prayer.
9. Listening silently to the khutbah is required; talking is forbidden.
10. Trade must stop at the call to prayer, and may resume after (Q 62:9–10).
11. Missing three Jumu'ahs without excuse is strongly condemned (hadith).
12. Friday is the best day of the week (Sayyid al-Ayyam), with an hour in which supplications are answered.
